# Decision Trees

[Slides for this lecture](10-decision-trees_slides.html)

```{r packages}
#| include: false
library("tidyverse")
library("rpart")
library("rpart.plot")
theme_set(theme_bw())
set.seed(20261031)

# Printed output wraps at 80 characters.
options(width = 80)

# Fixed decimals with thousands separators, for use inside $...$, whose
# hyphen MathJax sets as a minus. Adding 0 after rounding turns a negative
# zero into 0.
fmt_math <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  rounded <- round(x, digits) + 0
  formatC(rounded, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
}

# The same for prose, where a negative value prints with a minus sign (the
# HTML entity) rather than a hyphen.
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  sub("^-", "&minus;", fmt_math(x, digits))
}

# A percentage, for prose.
pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  paste0(fmt(100 * x, digits), "%")
}

# A count with thousands separators, for prose.
big <- function(x) {
  format(x, big.mark = ",")
}

# "a", "a and b", "a, b, and c".
and_list <- function(x) {
  n_x <- length(x)
  if (n_x == 1) {
    return(x)
  }
  if (n_x == 2) {
    return(paste(x, collapse = " and "))
  }
  paste0(paste(x[-n_x], collapse = ", "), ", and ", x[n_x])
}

# A cut point as rpart() chooses it, a midpoint of two recorded values,
# with at most two decimals and no trailing zeros, for prose.
cut_text <- function(x) {
  as.character(round(x, 2))
}

# A name set as code in prose.
code <- function(x) {
  paste0("`", x, "`")
}

# Mean squared error of predictions y_hat of responses y.
mse <- function(y, y_hat) {
  mean((y - y_hat)^2)
}

# Number of leaves of a tree.
n_leaves <- function(fit) {
  sum(fit$frame$var == "<leaf>")
}

# Color-blind-friendly palette.
okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00",
               "#56B4E9",
               "#009E73",
               "#D55E00",
               "#0072B2",
               "#CC79A7")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### Learning objectives
After this lecture you should be able to

- **describe** a regression tree as a partition of the values of the
explanatory variables into regions $R_1, \ldots, R_J$, with the mean training
response of a region as the prediction for every observation in it, and
**read** a prediction from a fitted tree's printout or diagram,
- **derive** the best single split, the explanatory variable $j$ and cut
point $s$ that minimize the summed RSS of the two regions, **show** that the
decrease in RSS is
$n_1n_2\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y_2\right)^2/\left(n_1 + n_2\right)$, and
**explain** why recursive binary splitting is greedy and top-down,
- **explain** cost-complexity pruning, the criterion
$\text{RSS} + \alpha|T|$ and its nested sequence of subtrees, **choose**
$\alpha$ by 10-fold cross-validation, and **evaluate** the pruned tree on
test data,
- **compute** the classification error rate, the Gini index, and the entropy
of a node and of a split, and **explain** why the Gini index or the entropy,
not the error rate, is used to grow a classification tree,
- **fit** regression and classification trees with `rpart()`, prune them
with `prune()`, and **evaluate** them by test MSE or by a test confusion
matrix, and
- **compare** trees with linear models: interpretability, nonlinearity and
interactions without feature engineering, predictions that are piecewise
constant, and high variance.
:::

Most models so far have been linear in a set of features, with any
curvature or interaction built into the features by hand. A **decision
tree** instead splits the values of the explanatory variables into
rectangles and predicts a constant in each. It needs no features built by
hand: each split is on one explanatory variable as recorded. This lecture
grows trees for a numeric response (regression trees) and for a class
(classification trees), and prunes them back. The reading is
ISLR2 Section 8.1.

## Concrete strength

### Data

**Question.** How well do the ingredients of a concrete mix and its age
predict how much load the concrete can bear?

**Data.** `modeldata::concrete` records laboratory tests of concrete
cylinders (Yeh 2006, "Analysis of Strength of Concrete Using Design of
Experiments and Neural Networks," *Journal of Materials in Civil
Engineering* 18). Each observation is a **specimen**: one cylinder of one mix,
crushed at one age. The response is the compressive strength,
`compressive_strength`, in megapascals (MPa). The explanatory variables are
the amounts of seven ingredients, in kg per cubic meter of mix, and the age
of the specimen in days.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r cleaning}
#| output: false
# All rows, and the explanatory variables.
concrete <- modeldata::concrete
n_rows <- nrow(concrete)
explanatory <- setdiff(names(concrete), "compressive_strength")
p <- length(explanatory)

# Rows that repeat an earlier row exactly, and rows that repeat the mix and
# age of an earlier row with a different strength.
n_exact <- sum(duplicated(concrete))
n_same_mix <- sum(duplicated(select(concrete, all_of(explanatory))))
n_replicate <- n_same_mix - n_exact

# One row per specimen.
specimens <- distinct(concrete)
n_specimens <- nrow(specimens)

# The ages at which specimens were tested.
ages <- sort(unique(specimens$age))
```
:::

The `r big(n_rows)` rows include `r n_exact` that repeat an earlier row
exactly, strength included. These are treated as duplicated records of one
specimen, and `distinct()` removes them so that no specimen is both a
training and a test specimen. Another `r n_replicate` rows repeat the mix and
age of an earlier row with a different strength; they are separate specimens
and stay. That leaves `r big(n_specimens)` specimens, tested at
`r length(ages)` ages from `r min(ages)` to `r max(ages)` days.

### Training specimens

```{r split}
# The training sample size.
n_train <- 700

# Training specimens: a random sample; every other specimen is a test
# specimen.
train_id <- sample(n_specimens, n_train)
train <- specimens[train_id, ]
test <- specimens[-train_id, ]
```

The split leaves `r n_train` training specimens and
`r nrow(test)` test specimens. The figure plots the strength of each training
specimen against its age, on a log scale, and against its cement content.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r data-plots}
#| output: false
# Ages repeat, so each training specimen's age is jittered once, by up to
# 8% either way, and the jittered age is used in every figure.
jitter_factor <- 0.08
train_plot <- train |>
  mutate(age_jit = age * exp(runif(n(), -jitter_factor, jitter_factor)))

# Age on a log scale: major lines at 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200 days,
# no minor lines; the limits run past the youngest and oldest specimens.
age_limits <- c(0.8, 450)
age_axis <- scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200),
                          minor_breaks = NULL,
                          limits = age_limits,
                          expand = expansion(0))

# Cement: major lines every 100 kg per cubic meter, minor lines midway.
cement_limits <- c(100, 550)
cement_axis <- scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(100, 500, by = 100),
                                  minor_breaks = seq(150, 550, by = 100),
                                  limits = cement_limits,
                                  expand = expansion(0))

# Strength: major lines every 20 MPa, minor lines midway.
strength_axis <- scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 80, by = 20),
                                    minor_breaks = seq(10, 90, by = 20),
                                    limits = c(0, 90))

# Strength against age and against cement, side by side.
title_train <- paste(n_train, "training specimens")
strength_age <- ggplot(train_plot,
                       aes(x = age_jit, y = compressive_strength)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  age_axis +
  strength_axis +
  labs(x = "Age (days, log scale)", y = "Compressive strength (MPa)")
strength_cement <- ggplot(train, aes(x = cement,
                                     y = compressive_strength)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  cement_axis +
  strength_axis +
  labs(x = "Cement (kg per cubic meter)", y = NULL)
data_plot <- patchwork::wrap_plots(strength_age, strength_cement) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(title = title_train)

# Mean strength at 3 and at 28 days, and the share of specimens at 28 days.
age_means <- train |>
  summarise(strength = mean(compressive_strength), .by = age)
mean_at <- function(a) {
  age_means$strength[age_means$age == a]
}
share_28 <- mean(train$age == 28)

# Share of the test specimens whose mix, the seven ingredients, is the mix
# of some training specimen.
ingredients <- setdiff(explanatory, "age")
train_mixes <- distinct(select(train, all_of(ingredients)))
mix_seen <- semi_join(test, train_mixes, by = ingredients)
share_mix_seen <- nrow(mix_seen) / nrow(test)
```
:::

```{r data-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
data_plot
```

Strength rises steeply with age over the first month, from a mean of
`r fmt(mean_at(3), 1)` MPa at 3 days to `r fmt(mean_at(28), 1)` MPa at 28
days, and more slowly, and noisily, afterward; `r pct(share_28, 0)` of the
training specimens were tested at 28 days, the standard age for testing
concrete. Strength rises with cement too, with a wide spread at every cement
content: specimens with the same cement differ in age and in the other six
ingredients. The relation with age is far from a straight line, and a linear
model would need features, such as a log of age, built for that curvature.

Many mixes were tested at several ages: `r pct(share_mix_seen, 0)` of the
test specimens have a mix, the seven ingredients, that some training
specimen also has. The test MSEs below therefore measure predictions for
mixes like those tested, often at a new age, not for mixes never tested.

## Regression trees

### Age and cement

The figure plots the training specimens by their age and their cement
content, with color showing strength.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r plane-plot}
#| output: false
# Cement on the vertical axis, with the same limits and grid lines.
cement_y_axis <- scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(100, 500, by = 100),
                                    minor_breaks = seq(150, 550, by = 100),
                                    limits = cement_limits,
                                    expand = expansion(0))

# Strength as color, on the viridis scale, which also runs from dark to
# light; legend marks every 20 MPa.
strength_color <- scale_color_viridis_c(breaks = seq(0, 80, by = 20),
                                        limits = c(0, 90))
plane_plot <- ggplot(train_plot, aes(x = age_jit, y = cement,
                                     color = compressive_strength)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  strength_color +
  age_axis +
  cement_y_axis +
  labs(x = "Age (days, log scale)", y = "Cement (kg per cubic meter)",
       color = "Strength\n(MPa)", title = title_train)
```
:::

```{r plane-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
plane_plot
```

The dark, weak specimens sit at the left, at young ages, and in the bottom
band of low cement; the light, strong ones sit at the right and the top. A
vertical line near 3 weeks and a horizontal line or two in cement would
already separate much of the weak concrete from the strong.

### Regions and predictions

A regression tree turns those lines into a model. It divides the values of
the explanatory variables into $J$ non-overlapping rectangles, the regions
$R_1, \ldots, R_J$, and predicts the mean training response of a region for
every observation that falls in it:

$$\hat f(x) = \sum_{m=1}^{J} \hat y_{R_m}\,\mathrm{I}\left(x \in R_m\right),$$

where

- $x$ is a value of the $p$ explanatory variables $X = (X_1, \ldots, X_p)$,
- $R_m$ is the $m$th region, a rectangle in the $p$ explanatory variables,
- $\hat y_{R_m}$ is the mean response of the training observations in $R_m$,
and
- $\mathrm{I}\left(x \in R_m\right)$ is 1 if $x$ falls in $R_m$ and 0 otherwise.

A tree splits on the explanatory variables as recorded, so in this chapter
each feature is an explanatory variable. Observation $i$ has values
$x_i = (x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ip})$, with $x_{ij}$ the value of explanatory
variable $X_j$, and response $y_i$.

For given regions, the tree's training RSS is

$$\text{RSS} = \sum_{m=1}^{J}\sum_{i:\, x_i \in R_m}\left(y_i - \hat y_{R_m}\right)^2.$$

Within one region, $\sum_{i:\, x_i \in R_m}\left(y_i - c\right)^2$ has
derivative $-2\sum_{i:\, x_i \in R_m}\left(y_i - c\right)$ in $c$, which is
zero at the region's mean, so the mean is the constant with the smallest RSS in
that region. The regions themselves are harder: there are too many ways to
partition the values into rectangles to search them all, so a tree builds its
regions one split at a time.

### Best split

A split of a region $R$ on explanatory variable $j$ at cut point $s$ makes
two regions,

$$R_1(j, s) = \left\{X \in R \mid X_j < s\right\}, \qquad R_2(j, s) = \left\{X \in R \mid X_j \ge s\right\},$$

where

- $R$ is the region being split (at the first split, every value of the
explanatory variables),
- $X_j$ is explanatory variable $j$, and
- $s$ is the cut point.

The best split is the pair $(j, s)$ that minimizes

$$\sum_{i:\, x_i \in R_1(j, s)}\left(y_i - \hat y_{R_1}\right)^2 + \sum_{i:\, x_i \in R_2(j, s)}\left(y_i - \hat y_{R_2}\right)^2,$$

the RSS of the two regions after the split.

Write $n_1$ and $n_2$ for the numbers of training observations in the two
regions, $\bar y_1 = \hat y_{R_1}$ and $\bar y_2 = \hat y_{R_2}$ for their
means, $n_R = n_1 + n_2$ for the number in the region being split (the training
sample size $n$ only at the first split), and
$\bar y = \left(n_1\bar y_1 + n_2\bar y_2\right)/n_R$ for the mean before the
split. In $R_1$,
$\sum\left(y_i - \bar y\right)^2 = \sum\left(y_i - \bar y_1\right)^2 + n_1\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y\right)^2$,
because the cross term
$2\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y\right)\sum\left(y_i - \bar y_1\right)$ is zero, and
likewise in $R_2$. Since
$\bar y_1 - \bar y = n_2\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y_2\right)/n_R$ and
$\bar y_2 - \bar y = -n_1\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y_2\right)/n_R$, the RSS before
the split minus the RSS after it is

$$n_1\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y\right)^2 + n_2\left(\bar y_2 - \bar y\right)^2 = \frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y_2\right)^2.$$

The best split separates two means as far apart as possible, weighted toward
regions of similar size. The RSS after the split changes only when $s$
crosses an observed value of $X_j$, so only the cut points between
consecutive distinct values need checking: at most $n_R - 1$ for each
explanatory variable. `rpart()` uses the midpoints.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r split-search}
#| output: false
# Decrease in RSS, as a share of the RSS before the split, for every cut
# point of explanatory variable v: the midpoints of its distinct values.
split_curve <- function(data, v, y = "compressive_strength") {
  values <- sort(unique(data[[v]]))
  cuts <- (head(values, -1) + tail(values, -1)) / 2
  response <- data[[y]]
  rss_before <- sum((response - mean(response))^2)
  decrease <- map_dbl(cuts, \(s) {
    left <- data[[v]] < s
    n_1 <- sum(left)
    n_2 <- sum(!left)
    gap <- mean(response[left]) - mean(response[!left])
    n_1 * n_2 / (n_1 + n_2) * gap^2
  })
  tibble(variable = v, cut = cuts, share = decrease / rss_before)
}

# Every cut point of every explanatory variable at the root, and the best
# cut point of each explanatory variable.
root_curves <- map(explanatory, \(v) split_curve(train, v)) |>
  list_rbind()
root_best <- root_curves |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE, by = variable) |>
  arrange(desc(share))
best_age <- filter(root_best, variable == "age")
best_cement <- filter(root_best, variable == "cement")

# Share of the RSS removed: major lines every 10%, minor lines midway.
share_axis <- scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 0.4, by = 0.1),
                                 minor_breaks = seq(0.05, 0.35, by = 0.1),
                                 limits = c(0, 0.35),
                                 labels = scales::label_percent())

# The curves for age and cement, the best cut point of each circled.
curve_panel <- function(v) {
  curve <- filter(root_curves, variable == v)
  best <- filter(root_best, variable == v)
  ggplot(curve, aes(x = cut, y = share)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 1) +
    geom_point(data = best, size = 4, shape = 1) +
    share_axis
}
age_curve <- curve_panel("age") +
  age_axis +
  labs(x = "Cut point s on age (days, log scale)",
       y = "Share of RSS removed")
cement_curve <- curve_panel("cement") +
  cement_axis +
  labs(x = "Cut point s on cement (kg per cubic meter)", y = NULL)
curve_plot <- patchwork::wrap_plots(age_curve, cement_curve) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(title = title_train,
                             caption = "Circles: the best cut point.")
```
:::

The figure plots, for every cut point $s$ on age and on cement, the share of
the training RSS that the split of all `r n_train` training specimens
removes.

```{r curve-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
curve_plot
```

The best split on age is at $s = `r cut_text(best_age$cut)`$ days, which
removes `r pct(best_age$share)` of the RSS; the best split on cement is at
$s = `r cut_text(best_cement$cut)`$ kg per cubic meter, which removes
`r pct(best_cement$share)`. With specimens tested at only `r length(ages)`
ages, age has only `r length(ages) - 1` cut points to check. Over all `r p`
explanatory variables, the best first split is on
`r code(root_best$variable[1])`, with
`r code(root_best$variable[2])` next
(`r pct(root_best$share[2])`).

### Recursive binary splitting

A tree repeats the best split inside each region it creates:

1. Start with all the training observations in one region, the **root**.
2. In each current region, find the best split $(j, s)$ of the training
observations in that region alone, and split.
3. Repeat in each new region until a stopping rule holds.

The search is **greedy**: each split is the best one at its own step, chosen
without looking ahead to the splits it makes possible later. It is
**top-down**: it starts from the root and works down. The regions at the end
are the **leaves**, or terminal nodes; the splits are the internal nodes.

`rpart()` stops splitting a region when it holds fewer than
`r rpart.control()$minsplit` training observations, when a split would leave
a leaf with fewer than `r rpart.control()$minbucket`, or when the best split
would lower the tree's RSS by less than `r pct(rpart.control()$cp, 0)` of the
RSS of the root, the default **complexity parameter** `cp`. These are
defaults, chosen for speed; the Pruning section that follows chooses the
tree's size from the data instead. The tree `rpart()` grows with these
defaults is called the **default tree** below.

### Fitting

```{r two-fit}
# The default tree on age and cement.
two_fit <- rpart(compressive_strength ~ age + cement, data = train)
two_fit
```

Each line is a node: its number, the split that leads to it, its number of
training specimens, its RSS (`deviance`), and its mean strength (`yval`).
An asterisk marks a leaf. Node 1, the root, holds all `r n_train` specimens,
with mean `r fmt(two_fit$frame$yval[1], 1)` MPa. The first split sends the
specimens younger than `r cut_text(best_age$cut)` days to node 2 and the rest to
node 3, and each node $m$ has children $2m$ and $2m + 1$. A specimen's
prediction is the mean of the leaf it reaches. The tree has
`r n_leaves(two_fit)` leaves.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r draw-tree}
#| output: false
# The variable and cut point of each internal node: the primary split of
# each internal node comes first in its block of rows of fit$splits.
node_splits <- function(fit) {
  frame <- fit$frame
  internal <- frame$var != "<leaf>"
  block <- 1 + frame$ncompete[internal] + frame$nsurrogate[internal]
  first_row <- cumsum(c(1, head(block, -1)))
  tibble(node = as.integer(rownames(frame)[internal]),
         variable = as.character(frame$var[internal]),
         cut = fit$splits[first_row, "index"])
}

# Split labels with exact cut points: rpart.plot() otherwise rounds them to
# the digits of the node values.
exact_labels <- function(fit) {
  # rpart.plot() labels each node with the split that leads to it, the
  # split of its parent, node %/% 2; the root has none.
  splits <- node_splits(fit)
  nodes <- as.integer(rownames(fit$frame))
  parent_cut <- splits$cut[match(nodes %/% 2, splits$node)]
  function(x, labs, digits, varlen, faclen) {
    exact <- str_replace(labs, "[0-9.]+$", as.character(parent_cut))
    if_else(is.na(parent_cut), labs, exact)
  }
}

# Draw a tree: each node shows its mean (or class) and its share of the
# training observations; splits are written below the nodes.
draw_tree <- function(fit, box.palette = "Grays", ...) {
  rpart.plot(fit, type = 2, roundint = FALSE, box.palette = box.palette,
             split.fun = exact_labels(fit), ...)
}
```
:::

The diagram draws the same tree. Each box shows a node's mean strength and
its share of the training specimens; a specimen goes left when the
condition under the box holds.

```{r two-tree-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
draw_tree(two_fit, digits = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### For example,
A specimen of 28 days with 300 kg of cement per cubic meter is at least
`r cut_text(best_age$cut)` days old, so it goes right at the root; from there
it follows the cement and age conditions down to a leaf. Its prediction is
`r fmt(predict(two_fit, tibble(age = 28, cement = 300)), 1)` MPa, the mean
strength of the training specimens in that leaf.
:::

### Partition

The tabs draw the tree's regions over the training specimens, one level of
splits at a time; the last tab is the whole fitted tree. Each rectangle is
a leaf, labeled with its mean strength.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r partition-plots}
#| output: false
# The rectangle of each leaf of a tree on two explanatory variables, from
# the conditions on the path to the leaf, within the given limits.
leaf_rectangles <- function(fit, limits) {
  is_leaf <- fit$frame$var == "<leaf>"
  leaves <- as.integer(rownames(fit$frame)[is_leaf])
  paths <- path.rpart(fit, nodes = leaves, print.it = FALSE)
  rectangles <- map(paths, \(conditions) {
    bounds <- limits
    for (condition in conditions[-1]) {
      parts <- str_match(condition, "^(\\w+)\\s*(<|>=)\\s*(.+)$")
      v <- parts[2]
      s <- as.numeric(parts[4])
      if (parts[3] == "<") {
        bounds[[v]][2] <- min(bounds[[v]][2], s)
      } else {
        bounds[[v]][1] <- max(bounds[[v]][1], s)
      }
    }
    tibble(xmin = bounds[[1]][1], xmax = bounds[[1]][2],
           ymin = bounds[[2]][1], ymax = bounds[[2]][2])
  })
  list_rbind(rectangles) |>
    mutate(node = leaves, value = fit$frame$yval[is_leaf])
}

# The tree cut back to its first `depth` levels of splits: node m is at
# depth floor(log2(m)), and the internal nodes at `depth` become leaves.
first_levels <- function(fit, depth) {
  nodes <- as.integer(rownames(fit$frame))
  internal <- fit$frame$var != "<leaf>"
  toss <- nodes[internal & floor(log2(nodes)) == depth]
  if (length(toss) == 0) {
    return(fit)
  }
  snip.rpart(fit, toss = toss)
}

# Regions of a tree on age and cement, shaded and labeled by their means,
# over the specimens it was fit to.
concrete_limits <- list(age = age_limits, cement = cement_limits)
strength_fill <- scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 90), guide = "none")
partition_plot <- function(fit, label_size = 3.5, data = train_plot,
                           title = title_train, min_height = 0) {
  rectangles <- leaf_rectangles(fit, concrete_limits) |>
    mutate(x = sqrt(xmin * xmax), y = (ymin + ymax) / 2)

  # Regions too thin for a label, in kg per cubic meter, go unlabeled.
  labeled <- filter(rectangles, ymax - ymin >= min_height)
  ggplot() +
    geom_rect(data = rectangles,
              aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
                  fill = value),
              alpha = 0.5, color = "black") +
    geom_point(data = data, aes(x = age_jit, y = cement),
               size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_label(data = labeled,
               aes(x = x, y = y, label = fmt(value, 1)),
               size = label_size, linewidth = 0, alpha = 0.8) +
    strength_fill +
    age_axis +
    cement_y_axis +
    labs(x = "Age (days, log scale)", y = "Cement (kg per cubic meter)",
         title = title)
}

# One plot per level of splits of the default tree.
two_depth <- max(floor(log2(as.integer(rownames(two_fit$frame)))))
level_plots <- map(seq_len(two_depth), \(d) {
  partition_plot(first_levels(two_fit, d))
})

# The tabs name five levels, the last the fitted tree; line up their panels.
stopifnot(two_depth == 5)
level_plots <- do.call(patchwork::align_patches, level_plots)
```
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r level-1-figure}
level_plots[[1]]
```

The fitted tree has `r two_depth` levels of splits, so its tab is the fifth
level. Every boundary is a vertical or horizontal line, and each later split
divides only the region it is made in: after the first split on age, the
young and the old specimens are split on cement at different cut points.
The fitted function is a step function in two explanatory variables,
constant on each rectangle and jumping at its edges.

## Pruning

### Overfitting

This section prunes the tree on age and cement only. With all `r p`
explanatory variables the full tree's test MSE is no worse than the pruned
tree's, as the All explanatory variables subsection below shows.

The default stopping rules ended the tree at `r n_leaves(two_fit)` leaves.
Growing it without them, until no region can be split, gives the **full
tree** $T_0$.

```{r full-fit}
# The full tree: no threshold on the decrease in RSS, and leaves as small
# as one specimen.
full_control <- rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 2, minbucket = 1)
full_fit <- rpart(compressive_strength ~ age + cement, data = train,
                  control = full_control)

# Number of leaves.
c(leaves = sum(full_fit$frame$var == "<leaf>"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r size-curve}
#| output: false
# The cross-validation table of the full tree, one row per subtree.
cp_table <- full_fit$cptable

# Training and test MSE of every subtree in the table.
y_train <- train$compressive_strength
y_test <- test$compressive_strength
size_curve <- map(seq_len(nrow(cp_table)), \(k) {
  subtree <- prune(full_fit, cp = cp_table[k, "CP"])
  tibble(leaves = cp_table[k, "nsplit"] + 1,
         Training = mse(y_train, predict(subtree, train)),
         Test = mse(y_test, predict(subtree, test)))
}) |>
  list_rbind()

# The subtree with the smallest test MSE, and the full tree.
test_best <- slice_min(size_curve, Test, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
full_row <- slice_tail(size_curve, n = 1)

# Number of leaves on a log scale: major lines at 1, 2, 5, 10, ..., 500, no
# minor lines.
leaves_axis <- scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500),
                             minor_breaks = NULL)

# MSE: major lines every 50, minor lines midway.
mse_axis <- scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 300, by = 50),
                               minor_breaks = seq(25, 325, by = 50),
                               limits = c(0, 300))
mse_labels <- c("Training", "Test")
size_long <- size_curve |>
  pivot_longer(-leaves, names_to = "data", values_to = "mse") |>
  mutate(data = factor(data, levels = mse_labels))
size_plot <- ggplot(size_long, aes(x = leaves, y = mse, color = data,
                                   linetype = data)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito[c(5, 4)]) +
  leaves_axis +
  mse_axis +
  labs(x = "Number of leaves |T| (log scale)", y = "MSE (MPa squared)",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL, title = title_train) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.02, 0.03),
        legend.justification = c(0, 0),
        legend.background = element_rect(color = "grey50"))
```
:::

The full tree has `r n_leaves(full_fit)` leaves for `r n_train` training
specimens. The figure plots the training and test MSE of the subtrees met
while pruning it back to the root, by their number of leaves.

```{r size-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
size_plot
```

The training MSE falls with every added leaf, to
`r fmt(full_row$Training, 1)` for the full tree; it is not zero because
specimens with the same age and cement but different other ingredients share
a leaf. The test MSE reaches its smallest value,
`r fmt(test_best$Test, 1)`, at `r test_best$leaves` leaves and is higher for
larger trees, `r fmt(full_row$Test, 1)` for the full tree. Its smallest
leaves hold one or a few specimens each, and their means follow those
specimens' other ingredients and measurement error, not a pattern that
recurs in the test specimens.

### Cost-complexity pruning

Stopping early is a poor remedy: a split that removes little RSS can lead to
splits below it that remove much more, and a stopping rule never sees them.
**Cost-complexity pruning** instead grows $T_0$ and cuts it back. For each
$\alpha \ge 0$ it finds the subtree $T \subseteq T_0$ that minimizes

$$C_\alpha(T) = \sum_{m=1}^{|T|}\sum_{i:\, x_i \in R_m}\left(y_i - \hat y_{R_m}\right)^2 + \alpha|T|,$$

where

- $T$ is a subtree of $T_0$, obtained by turning some internal nodes into
leaves (collapsing everything below them),
- $|T|$ is the number of leaves of $T$, and $R_m$ its $m$th leaf, and
- $\alpha$ is the tuning parameter, the RSS a leaf must remove to be worth
keeping.

With $\alpha = 0$ the minimizer is $T_0$, and as $\alpha$ grows it has fewer
leaves, down to the root alone. Like $\lambda$ in ridge regression and the
lasso, $\alpha$ trades the fit to the training data against a penalty on the
model; the penalty counts leaves, as the subset selection criteria count
features, rather than measuring the size of estimates. The minimizing
subtrees are **nested**: as $\alpha$ increases, the next subtree is found by
collapsing the internal node whose removal raises the RSS least per leaf
removed (**weakest link pruning**), so the whole sequence comes from one
pass over $T_0$, one subtree per row of the table below.

`rpart()` scales the tuning parameter by the RSS of the root: its complexity
parameter `cp` is $\alpha$ divided by the root's RSS, so a split is kept
only if it lowers the RSS by at least `cp` times the root's RSS. The default
`cp = `r rpart.control()$cp`` is the stopping rule of the default tree,
described under Recursive binary splitting.

### Cross-validation

While fitting, `rpart()` also runs 10-fold cross-validation over the
sequence of subtrees and stores the results in `cptable`, which `printcp()`
prints. The full tree's table has one row per subtree; the rows around the
smallest cross-validation estimate are

```{r cp-table}
# The full tree's table, and the rows around its smallest xerror.
cp_table <- full_fit$cptable
best_row <- which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"])
cp_table[best_row + (-2:2), ]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r cv-curve}
#| output: false
# The cross-validation estimate of the MSE: xerror is the cross-validation
# sum of squared errors divided by the root's RSS.
rss_root <- full_fit$frame$dev[1]
cv_curve <- tibble(leaves = cp_table[, "nsplit"] + 1,
                   cv = cp_table[, "xerror"] * rss_root / n_train)
cv_best <- cv_curve[best_row, ]

# The cross-validation estimate against the number of leaves, the chosen
# size circled, on the axes of the training and test MSE figure.
cv_plot <- ggplot(cv_curve, aes(x = leaves, y = cv)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = cv_best, size = 4, shape = 1) +
  leaves_axis +
  mse_axis +
  labs(x = "Number of leaves |T| (log scale)",
       y = "10-fold CV estimate (MPa squared)", title = title_train,
       caption = "Circle: the chosen number of leaves.")
```
:::

Each row is one subtree of the sequence: `CP` is the value of `cp` at which
it becomes the minimizer, `nsplit` its number of splits (one fewer than its
number of leaves), `rel error` its training RSS divided by the root's RSS,
and `xerror` its cross-validation sum of squared errors divided by the
root's RSS. `xstd` is a standard error of `xerror`. The figure plots the
cross-validation estimate of the MSE, `xerror` times the root's RSS divided
by $n$.

```{r cv-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
cv_plot
```

The estimate is smallest, `r fmt(cv_best$cv, 1)`, at `r cv_best$leaves`
leaves, and it rises for larger trees as the test MSE did. In each fold the
full tree is grown from the training folds and pruned with the same values
of `cp`, so the estimate for a value of `cp` judges the whole procedure, not
one particular tree.

### Pruned tree

```{r pruned-fit}
# Prune the full tree at the cp with the smallest xerror.
cp_best <- cp_table[best_row, "CP"]
pruned_fit <- prune(full_fit, cp = cp_best)

# Test MSE of the full and the pruned tree.
y_test <- test$compressive_strength
c(full = mean((y_test - predict(full_fit, test))^2),
  pruned = mean((y_test - predict(pruned_fit, test))^2))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r pruned-plot}
#| output: false
# Least squares on age and cement, for comparison.
two_ls <- lm(compressive_strength ~ age + cement, data = train)

# Test MSE of the trees and of least squares on age and cement.
two_mse <- c(ls = mse(y_test, predict(two_ls, test)),
             default = mse(y_test, predict(two_fit, test)),
             full = mse(y_test, predict(full_fit, test)),
             pruned = mse(y_test, predict(pruned_fit, test)))

# Regions of the pruned tree, with smaller labels, and none on regions
# less than 25 kg per cubic meter tall.
min_height <- 25
pruned_partition <- partition_plot(pruned_fit, label_size = 2.5,
                                   min_height = min_height) +
  labs(caption = paste("Regions less than", min_height,
                       "kg per cubic meter tall are not labeled."))

# The pruned tree's first split, which the prose says is the default
# tree's.
pruned_root <- node_splits(pruned_fit)[1, ]
default_root <- node_splits(two_fit)[1, ]
stopifnot(pruned_root$variable == default_root$variable,
          pruned_root$cut == default_root$cut)

# Share of the full tree's test MSE above the smallest of any subtree that
# pruning removes.
full_excess <- two_mse[["full"]] - test_best$Test
prune_gain <- (two_mse[["full"]] - two_mse[["pruned"]]) / full_excess

# How far the default tree's test MSE is above the smallest of any subtree,
# and a sentence for prose: within near_best counts as near the best size.
near_best <- 0.05
default_excess <- two_mse[["default"]] / test_best$Test - 1
default_text <- if (default_excess <= near_best) {
  paste0("The default tree's test MSE is within ", pct(default_excess, 0),
         " of that smallest value: here the default stopping rules ",
         "happened to stop near the best size.")
} else {
  paste0("The default tree's test MSE is ", pct(default_excess, 0),
         " above that smallest value.")
}
```
:::

The pruned tree has `r n_leaves(pruned_fit)` leaves and test MSE
`r fmt(two_mse[["pruned"]], 1)`, against `r fmt(two_mse[["full"]], 1)` for
the full tree, `r fmt(two_mse[["default"]], 1)` for the default tree with
`r n_leaves(two_fit)` leaves, and `r fmt(two_mse[["ls"]], 1)` for least
squares on age and cement, which fits a straight line in age to a curve.
The smallest test MSE of any subtree is `r fmt(test_best$Test, 1)`.
Pruning at the cross-validation choice removes `r pct(prune_gain, 0)` of the
full tree's excess over it. `r default_text` The figure draws the pruned
tree's regions.

```{r pruned-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
pruned_partition
```

The pruned tree's first split is the default tree's, on
`r code(pruned_root$variable)` at `r cut_text(pruned_root$cut)` days. Below it,
more steps in cement and age divide each side, and some regions are thin
bands of cement that hold a few specimens.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Beyond this course
- **One-standard-error rule.** A common alternative chooses the smallest
tree whose `xerror` is within one `xstd` of the smallest, trading a little
estimated error for a smaller tree.
- **The folds.** `rpart()` draws its folds at random, so the chosen size can
change with the seed; its `xval` argument also accepts a vector of fold
labels.
:::

### All explanatory variables

The same steps on all `r p` explanatory variables, the full tree grown and
pruned at the smallest cross-validation estimate:

```{r all-fit}
# Grow the full tree on every explanatory variable, then prune at the cp
# with the smallest cross-validation estimate.
all_full <- rpart(compressive_strength ~ ., data = train,
                  control = full_control)
all_cp <- all_full$cptable
all_best <- all_cp[which.min(all_cp[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
all_pruned <- prune(all_full, cp = all_best)
c(test_mse = mean((y_test - predict(all_pruned, test))^2))
```

For comparison, least squares on all `r p`, least squares with
$\log(\texttt{age})$ in place of age, and the default tree:

```{r all-compare}
# Least squares, least squares on log(age), and the default tree.
all_ls <- lm(compressive_strength ~ ., data = train)
log_ls <- lm(compressive_strength ~ . - age + log(age), data = train)
all_default <- rpart(compressive_strength ~ ., data = train)

# Their test MSEs.
fits <- list(ls = all_ls, log_ls = log_ls, default = all_default)
sapply(fits, \(fit) mean((y_test - predict(fit, test))^2))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r compare-table}
#| output: false
# Test MSE of least squares with log(age).
log_ls_mse <- mse(y_test, predict(log_ls, test))

# Test MSE of each method on both sets of explanatory variables.
all_mse <- c(ls = mse(y_test, predict(all_ls, test)),
             default = mse(y_test, predict(all_default, test)),
             full = mse(y_test, predict(all_full, test)),
             pruned = mse(y_test, predict(all_pruned, test)))
leaves_two <- c(NA, n_leaves(two_fit), n_leaves(full_fit),
                n_leaves(pruned_fit))
leaves_all <- c(NA, n_leaves(all_default), n_leaves(all_full),
                n_leaves(all_pruned))
leaves_text <- function(x) {
  if_else(is.na(x), "none", as.character(x))
}
compare <- tibble(Method = c("Least squares", "Default tree", "Full tree",
                             "Pruned tree"),
                  two_leaves = leaves_text(leaves_two),
                  two_mse = fmt(two_mse, 1),
                  all_leaves = leaves_text(leaves_all),
                  all_mse = fmt(all_mse, 1))
compare_columns <- c("Method",
                     "Leaves, age and cement",
                     "Test MSE, age and cement",
                     paste0("Leaves, all ", p),
                     paste0("Test MSE, all ", p))
compare_table <- knitr::kable(compare, col.names = compare_columns,
                              align = "lrrrr")

# How the pruned tree compares with least squares on log(age), for prose.
log_compare <- if (all_mse[["pruned"]] < log_ls_mse) {
  "does better"
} else {
  "comes close to this error"
}

# Root mean squared error of the pruned tree on all variables, and the
# standard deviation of the test strengths.
all_rmse <- sqrt(all_mse[["pruned"]])
test_sd <- sd(y_test)

# Subtree sizes whose cross-validation estimate is within 5% of the
# smallest.
near_share <- 0.05
all_leaves <- all_cp[, "nsplit"] + 1
all_near <- all_leaves[all_cp[, "xerror"] < (1 + near_share) *
                         min(all_cp[, "xerror"])]

# The prose says the full tree's test MSE is no worse than the pruned
# tree's.
stopifnot(all_mse[["full"]] <= all_mse[["pruned"]])

# Training specimens in each leaf of the full tree: leaves with one
# specimen, and, for the others, whether their specimens share an age,
# share all eight explanatory variables, and share a strength.
leaf_sizes <- table(all_full$where)
n_single <- sum(leaf_sizes == 1)
multi_leaves <- train |>
  mutate(leaf = all_full$where) |>
  filter(leaf %in% as.integer(names(leaf_sizes)[leaf_sizes > 1])) |>
  summarise(same_age = n_distinct(age) == 1,
            same_all = nrow(distinct(pick(all_of(explanatory)))) == 1,
            same_strength = n_distinct(compressive_strength) == 1,
            spread = max(map_dbl(pick(all_of(ingredients)),
                                 \(v) diff(range(v)))),
            .by = leaf)
n_multi <- nrow(multi_leaves)
n_same_all <- sum(multi_leaves$same_all)
n_same_strength <- sum(multi_leaves$same_strength)

# Leaves whose mixes differ by at most close_limit kg per cubic meter in
# every ingredient, how many of those have equal strengths, and the largest
# difference in the others.
close_limit <- 1
is_close <- multi_leaves$spread <= close_limit
n_close <- sum(is_close)
n_close_equal <- sum(is_close & multi_leaves$same_strength)
max_spread <- max(multi_leaves$spread)

# The prose says every leaf with several specimens shares an age.
stopifnot(all(multi_leaves$same_age))
```
:::

The table collects the test MSE of least squares and of the default, full,
and pruned trees, on age and cement and on all `r p` explanatory variables.

```{r compare-display}
#| echo: false
compare_table
```

With all `r p` explanatory variables, the pruned tree has
`r n_leaves(all_pruned)` leaves and test MSE `r fmt(all_mse[["pruned"]], 1)`,
a root mean squared error of `r fmt(all_rmse, 1)` MPa against a standard
deviation of `r fmt(test_sd, 1)` MPa among the test strengths. Least squares
on the same `r p` explanatory variables has test MSE
`r fmt(all_mse[["ls"]], 1)`. The default tree, stopped early by `rpart()`'s
stopping rules at `r n_leaves(all_default)` leaves, has test MSE
`r fmt(all_mse[["default"]], 1)`, against `r fmt(all_mse[["full"]], 1)` and
`r fmt(all_mse[["pruned"]], 1)` for the full and pruned trees grown past
it: the splits a stopping rule never reaches are where most of the gain
is.

Pruning changes little here. The cross-validation estimate is within
`r pct(near_share, 0)` of its smallest value for `r length(all_near)`
subtrees, with `r min(all_near)` to `r max(all_near)` leaves, so the choice
among large trees is loose, and the full tree's test MSE,
`r fmt(all_mse[["full"]], 1)`, is no worse than the pruned tree's. On age
and cement alone, specimens that share a small leaf still differ in six
ingredients the tree cannot see, and the full tree fits those differences.
With all `r p` recorded, `r n_single` of the full tree's
`r n_leaves(all_full)` leaves hold a single training specimen, and each of
the other `r n_multi` holds specimens of the same age. In `r n_close` of
those `r n_multi`, the mixes differ by at most `r close_limit` kg per cubic
meter in every ingredient (`r n_same_all` are identical), and
`r n_close_equal` of the `r n_close` have exactly equal strengths; in the
other `r n_multi - n_close`, some ingredient differs by up to
`r fmt(max_spread, 0)` kg per cubic meter. The full tree therefore predicts
a test specimen with the strength of a single training specimen, or the mean
of at most `r max(leaf_sizes)` specimens of the same age, usually with nearly
the same mix. That works here because `r pct(share_mix_seen, 0)` of the test
specimens have a mix that some training specimen also has, often at another
age. In this chapter, pruning helped more on age and cement alone, which
leave much of the strength unexplained, than on all `r p` explanatory
variables.

## Classification trees

### Penguin species

**Question.** Which of three species is a penguin, given four measurements
of its body?

**Data.** `modeldata::penguins` records `r nrow(modeldata::penguins)`
penguins of three species, Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo, from three islands
of the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Each observation is a **penguin**. The
response is `species`. The explanatory variables are four measurements:
bill length and bill depth (mm), flipper length (mm), and body mass (g).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r penguin-cleaning}
#| output: false
# The four measurements.
measurements <- c("bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm",
                  "body_mass_g")

# Penguins with no measurement at all, and the rest.
penguins_all <- modeldata::penguins
no_measurement <- penguins_all |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(measurements), is.na))
penguins <- penguins_all |>
  filter(!if_all(all_of(measurements), is.na))
n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)

# Penguins kept whose sex is missing, and any other missing measurement.
n_sex_missing <- sum(is.na(penguins$sex))
stopifnot(!anyNA(select(penguins, all_of(measurements))))
```
:::

`r nrow(no_measurement)` penguins have none of the four measurements and are
removed, leaving `r n_penguins`. Sex is missing for `r n_sex_missing` of
those; sex is not used, so they stay. Island is not used either, because a
split on a categorical variable is not covered in this lecture.

```{r penguin-split}
# The training sample size.
n_train_penguins <- 240

# Training penguins: a random sample; every other penguin is a test penguin.
penguin_id <- sample(n_penguins, n_train_penguins)
penguin_train <- penguins[penguin_id, ]
penguin_test <- penguins[-penguin_id, ]
```

That leaves `r n_train_penguins` training penguins and
`r nrow(penguin_test)` test penguins. The figure plots bill length against
flipper length for the training penguins, by species.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r penguin-plot}
#| output: false
# Species colors and shapes.
species_levels <- levels(penguins$species)
species_colors <- setNames(okabe_ito[c(1, 5, 3)], species_levels)
species_shapes <- setNames(c(16, 17, 15), species_levels)

# Flipper length: major lines every 10 mm, minor lines midway.
flipper_limits <- c(170, 235)
flipper_axis <- scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(170, 230, by = 10),
                                   minor_breaks = seq(175, 235, by = 10),
                                   limits = flipper_limits,
                                   expand = expansion(0))

# Bill length: major lines every 5 mm, minor lines midway.
bill_limits <- c(30, 60)
bill_axis <- scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 60, by = 5),
                                minor_breaks = seq(32.5, 57.5, by = 5),
                                limits = bill_limits,
                                expand = expansion(0))

# Bill length against flipper length, by species.
title_penguins <- paste(n_train_penguins, "training penguins")
penguin_plot <- ggplot(penguin_train,
                       aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
                           color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = species_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = species_shapes) +
  flipper_axis +
  bill_axis +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)", color = NULL,
       shape = NULL, title = title_penguins) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Training penguins of each species.
species_counts <- table(penguin_train$species)
```
:::

```{r penguin-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
penguin_plot
```

The training penguins are `r species_counts[["Adelie"]]` Adelie,
`r species_counts[["Chinstrap"]]` Chinstrap, and
`r species_counts[["Gentoo"]]` Gentoo. Gentoo penguins have the longest
flippers, and among the shorter-flippered penguins Chinstrap penguins have
longer bills than Adelie penguins. One vertical line and one horizontal
line in the left part of the plot would separate the three species, with a
few penguins on the wrong side.

### Most common class

A classification tree splits the explanatory variables into regions in the
same way, and predicts for a region its most common class among the
training observations in it. The class proportions in a region are

$$\hat p_{mk} = \frac{1}{n_m}\sum_{i:\, x_i \in R_m}\mathrm{I}\left(y_i = k\right),$$

where

- $K$ is the number of classes, here $K = `r nlevels(penguins$species)`$,
indexed $k = 1, \ldots, K$,
- $n_m$ is the number of training observations in region $R_m$, and
- $\hat p_{mk}$ is the proportion of them in class $k$.

The prediction for region $R_m$ is the class $k$ with the largest
$\hat p_{mk}$, and the proportions themselves estimate the probability of
each class for an observation in $R_m$.

### Node impurity

A regression tree chooses the split with the smallest RSS. A classification
tree chooses the split with the smallest **impurity**, a measure of how
mixed the classes in a region are. Three measures of the impurity of region
$m$ are

$$E_m = 1 - \max_k \hat p_{mk}, \qquad G_m = \sum_{k=1}^K \hat p_{mk}\left(1 - \hat p_{mk}\right), \qquad D_m = -\sum_{k=1}^K \hat p_{mk}\log \hat p_{mk},$$

where

- $E_m$ is the **classification error rate**, the share of the region's
training observations not in its most common class,
- $G_m$ is the **Gini index**, and
- $D_m$ is the **entropy**, with the natural log and $0\log 0 = 0$.

All three are zero when every observation in the region is in one class
(a **pure** node), and largest when the classes are equally common. The
impurity of a split is the average of the impurities of its two regions,
weighted by their numbers of observations,
$\left(n_1 Q_1 + n_2 Q_2\right)/\left(n_1 + n_2\right)$, where $Q$ is any
of the three measures and $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are its values in the two regions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r impurity-table}
#| output: false
# The three impurity measures of a vector of class proportions.
error_rate <- function(prop) {
  1 - max(prop)
}
gini <- function(prop) {
  sum(prop * (1 - prop))
}
entropy <- function(prop) {
  positive <- prop[prop > 0]
  -sum(positive * log(positive))
}

# Class counts and the three impurities of a set of penguins.
node_row <- function(node, species) {
  counts <- table(species)
  prop <- counts / sum(counts)
  tibble(Node = node, Adelie = counts[["Adelie"]],
         Chinstrap = counts[["Chinstrap"]], Gentoo = counts[["Gentoo"]],
         n = sum(counts), error = error_rate(prop), gini = gini(prop),
         entropy = entropy(prop))
}

# Impurity removed by every cut point of measurement v, for the penguins in
# `data`, by one impurity measure: the impurity before the split minus the
# weighted impurity after it, as a share of the impurity before.
class_split_curve <- function(data, v, measure) {
  values <- sort(unique(data[[v]]))
  cuts <- (head(values, -1) + tail(values, -1)) / 2
  impurity <- function(species) {
    measure(table(species) / length(species))
  }
  before <- impurity(data$species)
  after <- map_dbl(cuts, \(s) {
    left <- data[[v]] < s
    (sum(left) * impurity(data$species[left]) +
       sum(!left) * impurity(data$species[!left])) / nrow(data)
  })
  # Rounding sets rounding error in an unchanged impurity to exactly 0.
  share <- round((before - after) / before, 12)
  tibble(variable = v, cut = cuts, share = share)
}

# The best Gini split of the training penguins over all four measurements.
root_gini <- map(measurements, \(v) {
  class_split_curve(penguin_train, v, gini)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
root_var <- root_gini$variable
root_cut <- root_gini$cut

# The root, its two children, and the weighted average of the children.
goes_left <- penguin_train[[root_var]] < root_cut
left_label <- paste("flipper <", root_cut)
right_label <- paste("flipper >=", root_cut)
node_rows <- bind_rows(node_row("Root", penguin_train$species),
                       node_row(left_label, penguin_train$species[goes_left]),
                       node_row(right_label,
                                penguin_train$species[!goes_left]))
weights <- node_rows$n[2:3] / node_rows$n[1]
split_row <- node_rows[2:3, ] |>
  summarise(across(c(error, gini, entropy), \(x) sum(weights * x))) |>
  mutate(Node = "Split (weighted)")
impurity_tibble <- bind_rows(node_rows, split_row) |>
  mutate(across(c(error, gini, entropy), \(x) fmt(x, 3)),
         across(c(Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo, n), \(x) {
           if_else(is.na(x), "", as.character(x))
         }))
impurity_table <- knitr::kable(impurity_tibble,
                               col.names = c("Node", "Adelie", "Chinstrap",
                                             "Gentoo", "n", "Error rate",
                                             "Gini index", "Entropy"),
                               align = "lrrrrrrr")

# Share of each impurity removed by the split.
share_removed <- function(measure) {
  1 - split_row[[measure]] / node_rows[[measure]][1]
}
```
:::

The best split of the training penguins by the Gini index is on
`r code(root_var)` at `r cut_text(root_cut)` mm. The table gives the class
counts and the three impurities of the root, of its two children, and of the
split.

```{r impurity-display}
#| echo: false
impurity_table
```

The right child is nearly pure Gentoo, and the left child holds nearly all
the Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. The split removes
`r pct(share_removed("error"), 0)` of the root's error rate,
`r pct(share_removed("gini"), 0)` of its Gini index, and
`r pct(share_removed("entropy"), 0)` of its entropy.

### Gini index and entropy

The figure plots, for every cut point on bill length within the left child,
the share of the left child's impurity that a split there removes, by each
measure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r impurity-curves}
#| output: false
# The penguins of the left child, and the three curves on bill length.
left_child <- penguin_train[goes_left, ]
measure_names <- c("Error rate", "Gini index", "Entropy")
measures <- list(error_rate, gini, entropy)
impurity_curves <- map2(measures, measure_names, \(measure, name) {
  class_split_curve(left_child, "bill_length_mm", measure) |>
    mutate(measure = name)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(measure = factor(measure, levels = measure_names))

# Cut points at which the error rate removes nothing but the Gini index
# removes some impurity.
error_flat <- impurity_curves |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = share) |>
  filter(`Error rate` <= 0, `Gini index` > 0)

# The prose says the error rate removes nothing at every cut point up to
# the largest of these.
low_error <- impurity_curves |>
  filter(measure == "Error rate", cut <= max(error_flat$cut))
stopifnot(all(low_error$share <= 0))

# Bill length: the left child's range, major lines every 5 mm, minor lines
# midway.
bill_x_axis <- scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 60, by = 5),
                                  minor_breaks = seq(32.5, 57.5, by = 5))

# Share removed: major lines every 20%, minor lines midway.
removed_axis <- scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2),
                                   minor_breaks = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.2),
                                   limits = c(0, 1),
                                   labels = scales::label_percent())
title_left <- paste(nrow(left_child), "training penguins with",
                    left_label, "mm")
impurity_plot <- ggplot(impurity_curves,
                        aes(x = cut, y = share, color = measure,
                            linetype = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito[c(4, 5, 3)]) +
  bill_x_axis +
  removed_axis +
  labs(x = "Cut point s on bill length (mm)",
       y = "Share of impurity removed", color = NULL, linetype = NULL,
       title = title_left) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::

```{r impurity-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
impurity_plot
```

All three measures are largest near the same cut point, which separates
Adelie from Chinstrap. Away from it they differ. At every cut point up to
`r cut_text(max(error_flat$cut))` mm the error rate removes nothing: both
regions keep Adelie as their most common class, so the count of penguins
outside it does not change. The Gini index and the entropy still fall at
those cut points, because one region becomes purer.

The reason is concavity. The class proportions of a region are the weighted
average of those of its two parts,
$\hat p_k = \left(n_1\hat p_{1k} + n_2\hat p_{2k}\right)/\left(n_1 + n_2\right)$,
with $\hat p_{1k}$ and $\hat p_{2k}$ the proportions of class $k$ in the two
parts. The Gini index and the entropy are strictly concave functions of the
proportions, so by Jensen's inequality the weighted impurity after a split is
smaller than before unless the two parts have the same proportions. The error
rate is concave but linear wherever the most common class stays the same, so a
split that leaves both parts with the parent's most common class does not lower
it. A tree grown on the error rate can stop at a split like that, while splits
below it would separate the classes. `rpart()` grows a classification tree with
the Gini index by default; `parms = list(split = "information")` uses the
entropy. The error rate is the usual measure for pruning, where the goal is
prediction accuracy.

### Fitting

```{r penguin-fit}
# A classification tree on the four measurements.
penguin_fit <- rpart(species ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
                       flipper_length_mm + body_mass_g,
                     data = penguin_train, method = "class")
print(penguin_fit, digits = 4)
```

```{r penguin-vars}
#| include: false
# The measurements the tree splits on, in the order of the frame.
penguin_vars <- setdiff(unique(as.character(penguin_fit$frame$var)),
                        "<leaf>")

# The first split is the best Gini split found in the impurity table.
stopifnot(as.character(penguin_fit$frame$var[1]) == root_var,
          abs(penguin_fit$splits[1, "index"] - root_cut) < 1e-8)
```

Each line gives a node's number of training penguins, the number not in its
most common class (`loss`), that class (`yval`), and the class proportions
$\hat p_{mk}$ in the order `r and_list(species_levels)`. The tree has
`r n_leaves(penguin_fit)` leaves and splits on
`r and_list(code(penguin_vars))`; `r code(setdiff(measurements, penguin_vars))`
is not used. Its first split is the one in the impurity table. The diagram
shows the most common class of each node, its class proportions, and its
share of the training penguins.

```{r penguin-tree-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
draw_tree(penguin_fit, extra = 104,
          box.palette = list("Oranges", "Blues", "Greens"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r penguin-partition}
#| output: false
# Regions of the penguin tree, shaded by their predicted species, over the
# training penguins.
penguin_limits <- list(flipper_length_mm = flipper_limits,
                       bill_length_mm = bill_limits)
species_of <- attr(penguin_fit, "ylevels")

# Node 3 is split on bill depth, which the plot does not show; it is drawn
# as one region.
penguin_plane <- snip.rpart(penguin_fit, toss = 3)
plane_vars <- setdiff(unique(as.character(penguin_plane$frame$var)),
                      "<leaf>")
stopifnot(all(plane_vars %in% names(penguin_limits)))
penguin_rectangles <- leaf_rectangles(penguin_plane, penguin_limits) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species_of[value], levels = species_levels))
penguin_partition <- ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = penguin_rectangles,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
                fill = species),
            alpha = 0.15, color = "black", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = penguin_train,
             aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
                 color = species, shape = species),
             size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = species_colors) +
  scale_color_manual(values = species_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = species_shapes) +
  flipper_axis +
  bill_axis +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)", color = NULL,
       shape = NULL, title = title_penguins) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::

The figure draws the tree's regions over the data plot, each shaded by its
predicted species. The region of long flippers is drawn as one rectangle:
its split on bill depth, a measurement the plot does not show, is left out.

```{r penguin-partition-figure}
#| echo: false

penguin_partition
```

### Test confusion matrix

```{r penguin-test}
# Predicted species of the test penguins, against their species.
penguin_pred <- predict(penguin_fit, penguin_test, type = "class")
confusion <- table(Predicted = penguin_pred,
                   Observed = penguin_test$species)
confusion
mean(penguin_pred == penguin_test$species)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r penguin-test-summary}
#| output: false
# Accuracy, misclassified test penguins, and the most common test species.
accuracy <- mean(penguin_pred == penguin_test$species)
n_wrong <- sum(penguin_pred != penguin_test$species)
majority_share <- max(table(penguin_test$species)) / nrow(penguin_test)
```
:::

The tree classifies `r pct(accuracy)` of the `r nrow(penguin_test)` test
penguins correctly and misclassifies `r n_wrong`. Predicting the most common
species for every penguin would be right for
`r pct(majority_share)` of them.

### Pruning

A classification tree is pruned in the same way, with the error rate in
place of the RSS in $C_\alpha(T)$. The rows of the full tree's table from
two above its smallest cross-validation estimate to the full tree are

```{r penguin-prune}
# The full classification tree, and its table from two rows above the
# smallest xerror.
penguin_full <- rpart(species ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
                        flipper_length_mm + body_mass_g,
                      data = penguin_train, method = "class",
                      control = full_control)
penguin_cp <- penguin_full$cptable
penguin_best <- which.min(penguin_cp[, "xerror"])
penguin_cp[max(1, penguin_best - 2):nrow(penguin_cp), ]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r penguin-prune-summary}
#| output: false
# The subtree with the smallest cross-validation estimate, and its test
# accuracy.
penguin_pruned <- prune(penguin_full, cp = penguin_cp[penguin_best, "CP"])
test_accuracy <- function(fit) {
  predicted <- predict(fit, penguin_test, type = "class")
  mean(predicted == penguin_test$species)
}
pruned_accuracy <- test_accuracy(penguin_pruned)

# Training penguins misclassified at the root, and in cross-validation by
# each subtree; the row of the subtree with the default tree's size.
train_counts <- table(penguin_train$species)
root_class <- names(which.max(train_counts))
root_errors <- n_train_penguins - max(train_counts)
cv_errors <- round(penguin_cp[, "xerror"] * root_errors)

# Every size that ties for the smallest estimate; which.min() takes the
# first, the smallest tree.
penguin_leaves <- penguin_cp[, "nsplit"] + 1
tied_leaves <- penguin_leaves[cv_errors == min(cv_errors)]
tie_text <- if (length(tied_leaves) > 1) {
  paste0(" (", and_list(tied_leaves), " leaves tie, and the smallest tree ",
         "is taken)")
} else {
  ""
}

# Whether the smallest estimate is at the full tree.
best_is_full <- penguin_best == nrow(penguin_cp)
if (best_is_full) {
  tie_text <- paste0(tie_text, ", the full tree itself, so here pruning ",
                     "removes nothing")
}

# Node 3's split in the default and the chosen tree, as code for prose,
# and the number of training penguins in node 6, its first child.
node_3_text <- function(fit) {
  split <- filter(node_splits(fit), node == 3)
  label <- labels(fit)[rownames(fit$frame) == "6"]
  op <- if (str_detect(label, ">=")) ">=" else "<"
  paste(split$variable, op, cut_text(split$cut))
}
node_6_size <- function(fit) {
  fit$frame$n[rownames(fit$frame) == "6"]
}
default_3 <- node_3_text(penguin_fit)
pruned_3 <- node_3_text(penguin_pruned)

# Test penguins each tree classifies correctly.
n_right <- function(fit) {
  predicted <- predict(fit, penguin_test, type = "class")
  sum(predicted == penguin_test$species)
}

# The prose compares two trees of the same size that differ only in node
# 3, whose chosen-tree child is smaller than the default minbucket allows.
minbucket <- rpart.control()$minbucket
stopifnot(n_leaves(penguin_pruned) == n_leaves(penguin_fit),
          default_3 != pruned_3,
          node_6_size(penguin_pruned) < minbucket)
```
:::

For a classification tree, `rel error` and `xerror` are numbers of
misclassified training penguins divided by the root's, the
`r root_errors` penguins that are not `r root_class`. The smallest
cross-validation estimate, `r cv_errors[penguin_best]` misclassified training
penguins, is at `r penguin_leaves[penguin_best]` leaves`r tie_text`;
the default tree has `r n_leaves(penguin_fit)`. The two trees differ in
node 3: the default tree splits it at `r code(default_3)`, leaving a leaf of
`r node_6_size(penguin_fit)` penguins, and the chosen tree at
`r code(pruned_3)`, leaving a leaf of `r node_6_size(penguin_pruned)`, which
the default `minbucket = `r minbucket`` forbids. The chosen tree classifies
`r pct(pruned_accuracy)` of the test penguins correctly, against
`r pct(accuracy)` for the default tree, `r n_right(penguin_pruned)` of
`r nrow(penguin_test)` against `r n_right(penguin_fit)`.

## Strengths and weaknesses

### Interpretability

A small tree is a list of rules a reader can follow without software: the
default concrete tree on age and cement has `r n_leaves(two_fit)` leaves, and
the default penguin tree `r n_leaves(penguin_fit)`. A classification tree
handles any number of classes with no change to the method. Interpretability
fades with size: the pruned tree on all `r p` explanatory variables has
`r n_leaves(all_pruned)` leaves, more than anyone reads.

### Nonlinearity and interactions

A tree needs no features built for curvature or interaction. On all `r p`
explanatory variables the pruned tree's test MSE was
`r fmt(all_mse[["pruned"]], 1)`, against `r fmt(all_mse[["ls"]], 1)` for
least squares. Least squares with $\log(\texttt{age})$ in place of age, a
feature chosen after seeing the curve in the data plot, has test MSE
`r fmt(log_ls_mse, 1)`; the tree `r log_compare` without being told about
the curvature.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r branch-cuts}
#| output: false
# Whether node n is node a or lies below it.
is_below <- function(n, a) {
  depth_gap <- floor(log2(n)) - floor(log2(a))
  depth_gap >= 0 & floor(n / 2^depth_gap) == a
}

# Cement cut points below the young (node 2) and the old (node 3) branch.
two_splits <- node_splits(two_fit)
stopifnot(two_splits$variable[1] == "age",
          abs(two_splits$cut[1] - best_age$cut) < 1e-8)
cement_splits <- filter(two_splits, variable == "cement")
young_cuts <- sort(cement_splits$cut[is_below(cement_splits$node, 2)])
old_cuts <- sort(cement_splits$cut[is_below(cement_splits$node, 3)])
```
:::

A split on another variable below a split is an interaction. In the default
tree on age and cement, the specimens younger than
`r cut_text(best_age$cut)` days are split on cement at
`r and_list(cut_text(young_cuts))` kg per cubic meter, and the older ones at
`r and_list(cut_text(old_cuts))`: the step in strength that cement makes
depends on age.

### Step functions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r halves}
#| output: false
# Number of random halvings of the training specimens.
n_halvings <- 200

# For each halving, the default trees and least squares on age and cement
# fit to the two halves; their first splits, and the root mean squared
# difference of the two fits' predictions for the test specimens.
two_formula <- compressive_strength ~ age + cement
rms_gap <- function(a, b) {
  sqrt(mean((predict(a, test) - predict(b, test))^2))
}
halvings <- map(seq_len(n_halvings), \(b) {
  half <- sample(n_train, n_train / 2)
  tree_a <- rpart(two_formula, data = train[half, ])
  tree_b <- rpart(two_formula, data = train[-half, ])
  ls_a <- lm(two_formula, data = train[half, ])
  ls_b <- lm(two_formula, data = train[-half, ])
  tibble(halving = b,
         root_a = labels(tree_a)[2],
         root_b = labels(tree_b)[2],
         tree_gap = rms_gap(tree_a, tree_b),
         ls_gap = rms_gap(ls_a, ls_b),
         trees = list(list(tree_a, tree_b)),
         halves = list(half))
}) |>
  list_rbind()

# How often the first splits of the two halves agree, and the most common
# first split.
root_labels <- c(halvings$root_a, halvings$root_b)
root_counts <- sort(table(root_labels), decreasing = TRUE)
same_root <- mean(halvings$root_a == halvings$root_b)
mean_tree_gap <- mean(halvings$tree_gap)
mean_ls_gap <- mean(halvings$ls_gap)

# Predicted strength at 28 days for cement on a grid.
cement_grid <- tibble(age = 28, cement = seq(100, 550, by = 0.5))

# The first 20 halvings: predictions of their 40 trees at 28 days.
n_shown <- 20
shown_curves <- map(seq_len(n_shown), \(b) {
  map(1:2, \(h) {
    tree <- halvings$trees[[b]][[h]]
    mutate(cement_grid, strength = predict(tree, cement_grid),
           curve = paste(b, h))
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}) |>
  list_rbind()

# The default tree and least squares on all training specimens.
fit_curves <- bind_rows(
  mutate(cement_grid, strength = predict(two_fit, cement_grid),
         fit = "Default tree"),
  mutate(cement_grid, strength = predict(two_ls, cement_grid),
         fit = "Least squares")
) |>
  mutate(fit = factor(fit, levels = c("Default tree", "Least squares")))

# Training specimens tested at 28 days.
train_28 <- filter(train, age == 28)
title_28 <- paste(nrow(train_28), "training specimens tested at 28 days")

# Predicted strength against cement at 28 days, over those specimens.
step_base <- ggplot(train_28, aes(x = cement, y = compressive_strength)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  cement_axis +
  strength_axis +
  labs(x = "Cement (kg per cubic meter)",
       y = "Strength at 28 days (MPa)", title = title_28)
step_fits <- step_base +
  geom_line(data = fit_curves,
            aes(y = strength, color = fit, linetype = fit),
            linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito[c(5, 4)]) +
  labs(color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.99, 0.03),
        legend.justification = c(1, 0),
        legend.background = element_rect(color = "grey50"))
step_halves <- step_base +
  geom_line(data = shown_curves, aes(y = strength, group = curve),
            color = okabe_ito[5], alpha = 0.4)
step_aligned <- patchwork::align_patches(step_fits, step_halves)
```
:::

A **halving** splits the `r n_train` training specimens at random into two
halves of `r n_train / 2`. The tabs plot predicted strength at 28 days
against cement, over the training specimens tested at that age. The first
tab draws the default tree and least squares on age and cement, fit to all
`r n_train` training specimens; the second draws the default trees fit to
the `r 2 * n_shown` halves of `r n_shown` halvings.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Tree and least squares
```{r step-fits-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
step_aligned[[1]]
```

#### Trees on halves
```{r step-halves-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
step_aligned[[2]]
```
:::

The tree's prediction is flat between cut points and jumps at each one, so
two mixes on either side of a cut point get different predictions however
close they are, and two mixes far apart within a region get the same one.
Least squares draws a straight line through the same specimens.

### Instability

The trees on halves in the second tab above differ in where they put their steps
and how high each step is. The tabs draw the regions of the two trees of
one halving, each over its own half of the training specimens: the first
halving, in the order drawn, whose two trees split first in different
places.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code
```{r halves-partition}
#| output: false
# The first halving whose two trees split first in different places.
shown <- which(halvings$root_a != halvings$root_b)[1]

# Its two halves, and the regions of their trees.
first_half <- halvings$halves[[shown]]
title_half <- paste(n_train / 2, "training specimens")
half_plots <- map(1:2, \(h) {
  rows <- if (h == 1) first_half else -first_half
  partition_plot(halvings$trees[[shown]][[h]], data = train_plot[rows, ],
                 title = title_half)
})

# The first split and the number of leaves of each tree.
half_roots <- c(halvings$root_a[shown], halvings$root_b[shown])
half_leaves <- map_int(halvings$trees[[shown]], n_leaves)
```
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### First half
```{r half-1-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
half_plots[[1]]
```

#### Second half
```{r half-2-figure}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
half_plots[[2]]
```
:::

The tree on the first half splits first on `r code(half_roots[1])` and has
`r half_leaves[1]` leaves; the tree on the second half splits first on
`r code(half_roots[2])` and has `r half_leaves[2]`. Each later split is made
inside a region the first split creates, so the two partitions differ
throughout. Over `r n_halvings` random halvings, the two halves split first at
the same place `r pct(same_root, 0)` of the time; the most common first split,
`r code(names(root_counts)[1])`, is the first split of
`r pct(root_counts[[1]] / (2 * n_halvings), 0)` of the `r 2 * n_halvings`
trees. Their predictions for a test specimen differ by
`r fmt(mean_tree_gap, 1)` MPa on average (root mean square over the test
specimens, averaged over the halvings). Least squares fits to the same halves
differ by `r fmt(mean_ls_gap, 1)` MPa.

A tree has high variance: trees fit to different training samples, shown
here by the two halves of a halving, differ, because each split is chosen
from the data and a different first or second split changes every split
below it. The next lecture averages many trees to reduce that
variance.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Beyond this course
- **Missing values.** `rpart()` keeps an observation with a missing value
of the split's explanatory variable by sending it down a **surrogate
split**, a split on another explanatory variable that best mimics the
primary one; `print(summary(fit))` lists them.
- **Categorical explanatory variables.** A split on a categorical variable
sends a subset of its levels left and the rest right; for a numeric response
the levels can be ordered by their mean response, which reduces the search
to splits of that order.
- **Conditional inference trees.** The `partykit` package chooses each split
by a hypothesis test of association between the response and each
explanatory variable, which avoids favoring variables with many possible cut
points.
- **Other trees.** Trees with splits on linear combinations of the
explanatory variables, and trees with a linear model in each leaf, trade
some interpretability for smoother fits.
:::

## Conclusion

A decision tree divides the values of the explanatory variables into
rectangular regions and predicts a constant in each: the mean training
response of the region for a regression tree, and its most common class for
a classification tree, whose class proportions estimate the class
probabilities. It splits on the explanatory variables as recorded, so it
needs no features built by hand.

The regions are grown by recursive binary splitting, a greedy, top-down
search. Each split chooses one explanatory variable and one cut point to
minimize the RSS of the two new regions, which is the same as maximizing
$n_1n_2\left(\bar y_1 - \bar y_2\right)^2/\left(n_1 + n_2\right)$, or,
for classes, to minimize
the weighted Gini index or entropy. Those two measures, unlike the
classification error rate, are strictly concave in the class proportions, so
they reward any split that makes a region purer.

A tree grown until its leaves are tiny can fit the training data too
closely; how much this costs depends on how much variation the explanatory
variables leave for small leaves to fit. Cost-complexity pruning cuts it
back by minimizing the training RSS (or error) plus $\alpha$ times the number
of leaves, which gives a nested sequence of subtrees from the full tree at
$\alpha = 0$ to the root. The tuning parameter, `cp` in `rpart()`, is chosen
by 10-fold cross-validation and the chosen tree evaluated once on test
data.

Trees are easy to read when they are small, capture nonlinearity and
interactions without feature engineering, and handle any number of classes.
Their predictions are step functions, and they have high variance: a
different training sample can change the first splits and, through them,
every region below.

The next lecture reduces that variance by averaging many trees: bagging fits
a tree to each of many bootstrap samples, and random forests also
restrict each split to a random subset of the explanatory variables.
